cards.front: What should you know about crude oil?
cards.back: is a mixture of hydrocarbons that formed from the remains of ancient biomass (mostly plankton) over millions of years under high pressure and temperature. It is a finite resource — it cannot be replaced once used.

cards.front: What should you know about fractional distillation?
cards.back: separates crude oil into fractions (groups of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points). The crude oil is heated and vapours rise up a fractionating column. Fractions condense at different heights depending on their boiling points .

cards.front: Recall a key point about Hydrocarbons And Crude Oil
cards.back: A hydrocarbon is a compound of carbon and hydrogen only . No other elements are present.

cards.front: What should you know about alkanes?
cards.back: are saturated hydrocarbons — they contain only single carbon–carbon bonds . The general formula for alkanes is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ .

cards.front: What should you know about alkenes?
cards.back: are unsaturated hydrocarbons — they contain a C=C double bond . The general formula for alkenes is CₙH₂ₙ . Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes because of the double bond.

cards.front: What should you know about bromine water test?
cards.back: for unsaturation: Add bromine water (orange) to the hydrocarbon. If it decolourises (goes colourless), the substance is an alkene (unsaturated). If it stays orange, it is an alkane (saturated).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Hydrocarbons And Crude Oil
cards.back: The properties of a hydrocarbon fraction depend on the length of the carbon chain .

cards.front: What should you know about cracking?
cards.back: breaks long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter, more useful molecules. It always produces at least one alkene (which has a C=C double bond) and an alkane.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Hydrocarbons And Crude Oil
cards.back: You need to use the general formulae CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (alkanes) and CₙH₂ₙ (alkenes) to work out molecular formulae, and balance cracking equations by ensuring the same number of C and H atoms on both sides.

cards.front: What should you know about answers?
cards.back: (a) Fuel oil has the greatest surplus (25% supply vs 5% demand = 20% surplus). Petrol has the greatest shortage (40% demand vs 15% supply = 25% shortage). (b) Cracking could break down surplus long-chain fractions (like fuel oil and bitumen) into shorter-chain fractions (like petrol) that are in high demand. This would reduce the surplus of fuel oil and help meet the demand for petrol. (c) The student is incorrect.
